title: Why did humans paint the walls of Lascaux?
subtitle: 15,000 BC
subject: art
description: In 1940, four teenagers and their dog found a cave near Montignac covered with bulls, horses and deer painted around 15,000 BC. Hunting magic, religious rite or a lesson for future hunters: the meaning of these images is still a mystery.
author: dusan-nikolic

hero.hook: Looking for a secret passage, four boys and their dog stumbled onto one of the greatest treasures of prehistoric art.

blocks.text: On **September 12, 1940**, four teenagers and their dog were walking in the woods near Montignac, in the Dordogne, when they noticed a hole in the ground. A local legend told of a secret passage leading to Lascaux Manor, so they crawled in. They found walls covered with horses, deer, stags, wild cattle, felines, a single human figure and strange shapes.
The four discoverers were not alone that day: their dog, whose name was Robot, was along for the walk.

They told their teacher, who alerted specialists in prehistoric art. Word spread, but scientists only turned their full attention to the cave after World War II. What a group of schoolboys stumbled upon by chance is today one of the most important sites of prehistoric art in the world. And one question hangs over these walls: why were they painted?

sections.title: Bulls, felines and a bird-headed man

blocks.text: To date, researchers have counted about **2,100 images** at Lascaux, painted or engraved, scattered throughout the cave. They have divided it into seven sections, three of them named after the figures found there. The largest is the [[Hall of the Bulls]], named after four great black bulls. Their scale is monumental: the longest measures **5.2 meters**.

blocks.caption: A red cow with a black head, surrounded by small horses: one of the Lascaux paintings.

blocks.text: The Shaft of the Dead Man takes its name from the only human figure in the cave: a man falling backward, killed by a wounded bison. One unsettling detail: his head is that of a bird. The Chamber of the Felines, the most remote part, is misnamed: most of its images are horses. From the moment of the discovery, one question gripped experts and public alike: who painted all this?

sections.title: Art, the signature of Homo sapiens

blocks.text: Painting a cave is what archaeologists call symbolic behavior. So far, figurative art, art that depicts beings and things, has been reliably recognized only in [[Homo sapiens]], anatomically modern humans. It requires the level of thinking needed for language, abstract thought and the passing on of knowledge.
Three caves in Spain occupied by [[Neanderthals]] carry linear signs, geometric shapes, hand stencils and handprints. No figurative art, however, has ever been attributed to them.

Archaeologists date the Lascaux paintings to around **15,000 BC**, at the very end of the [[Upper Paleolithic]]. Their makers most likely belonged to the [[Magdalenians]], hunter-gatherers spread across all of Western Europe: France, northern Spain, Switzerland, Germany, Belgium and southern Britain.

blocks.caption: A Magdalenian spear point made of bone or antler, seen from two sides, found at Bruniquel (Muséum de Toulouse).

blocks.text: These groups were skilled toolmakers who worked bone and reindeer antler. Their sites show an abundance of hunted animals and frequent contact with other groups. In short, these were well-fed, well-equipped and well-connected societies, with time to spare for making images.

No text accompanies these images: there was no writing in the Paleolithic. Yet Lascaux has become a reference point for understanding that world. The first researchers saw **hunting magic** in it: painting the animal on the wall would have helped to ensure a successful hunt.

blocks.caption: The Hall of the Bulls, reproduced at Lascaux II: a great black bull, red cows and horses before the visitors.

blocks.text: The bird-headed man of the Shaft led modern researchers down another path: a religious rite, or a form of [[shamanism]], a practice in which a person makes contact with the world of spirits. Wounded by the beast, the figure may also have served as a lesson, a way to **pass on knowledge** to future hunters.

Then there are the strange shapes and marks scattered all over the cave. They too have spawned all kinds of explanations, from an early form of writing to a technique for aiding memory. None of them has been proven so far.

In **1963**, the cave was closed to the public. Crowds of visitors and artificial lighting were destroying the paintings. Twenty years later, a faithful copy, [[Lascaux II]], opened next to the original. That effort of preservation says a great deal about the place Lascaux holds in the heritage of humanity.

blocks.text: The exact meaning of these images escapes us, and it probably always will. But their very existence tells us something universal. Long before the invention of writing, humans felt the need to communicate through images, and that need has never gone away.

Painted around 15,000 BC by Magdalenian Homo sapiens, the images of Lascaux keep their secret: hunting magic, rite or lesson, they prove above all that the urge to picture the world is as old as modern humanity.
